paragraphs: When matrix data arrives over time, an analysis may need to use only the most recent W updates. This sliding window requirement makes older information expire while new information enters. The paper studies how to perform useful matrix computations in this setting while also providing differential privacy.

The authors show that an existing framework for analysis without privacy does not withstand the noise needed for privacy. They develop a framework that tolerates this noise and use it to construct efficient private algorithms for spectral approximation, principal component analysis, multi-response linear regression, sparse PCA, and non-negative PCA. These algorithms use o(W) space, meaning that their memory grows more slowly than the window length.

The contribution covers several matrix tasks within one framework. The authors state that comparable results for private sparse and non-negative PCA were previously unavailable even for static data. They also establish a lower bound that identifies a cost of privacy in the sliding window setting, complementing their algorithmic results.
icml-2021-a-framework-for-private-matrix.tldr: A noise-robust framework enables differentially private matrix analysis using memory that grows sublinearly with the sliding window length.

paragraphs: Agents trained independently through self-play can develop policies that work with themselves but fail with unfamiliar partners. Zero-shot coordination asks how independently developed agents can nevertheless behave compatibly. This paper examines a proposed formulation in which players share a learning algorithm but cannot agree on labels for actions or observations.

The authors formalize that setting as label-free coordination, including a corresponding game. They show that other-play, previously proposed as optimal, can fail because its objective has multiple incompatible maximizers. Independently choosing among these equally good solutions does not reliably produce compatible behavior. An extension with tie-breaking resolves this issue: the authors prove that it is optimal for the formalized problem and an equilibrium of the associated game.

That success exposes a problem with the formulation itself. Arbitrary tie-breaking is something zero-shot coordination aims to avoid, yet the label-free problem permits a solution built around it. The paper therefore introduces an alternative informal description of the intended coordination challenge as a basis for future work.
icml-2021-a-new-formalism-method-and-ope.tldr: Formalizing label-free coordination reveals both a tie-breaking flaw in other-play and a mismatch between that formal problem and zero-shot coordination.

paragraphs: Optimizing an expensive black-box function requires choosing evaluations carefully because each query consumes resources. Bayesian optimization addresses this problem, and regret bounds describe how its optimization error decreases with additional evaluations. This paper asks whether combining Bayesian optimization with optimistic search can yield a faster decrease in a noise-free setting.

The proposed BOO algorithm combines Bayesian optimization ideas with methods that partition the search space. Its stated regret bound is O(N^(−√N)), where N is the number of evaluations. This result depends on a specific assumption: the objective is sampled from a Gaussian process with a Matérn kernel whose smoothness parameter satisfies ν > 4 + D/2, with D denoting the dimension.

The smoothness and noise-free requirements are central to interpreting the guarantee. Within that setting, the paper presents BOO as a practical approach achieving the stated rate. Experiments on synthetic functions and machine learning hyperparameter tuning also show better performance than the tested baselines, providing empirical support alongside the conditional theoretical result.
icml-2021-bayesian-optimistic-optimisati.tldr: BOO combines Bayesian optimization with partition-based optimistic search to obtain a rapidly decaying regret bound under specific noise-free smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to a black-box function by balancing exploration with exploitation. An acquisition function expresses that balance and determines which inputs are promising to evaluate next. Expected improvement is a common choice, but computing it often depends on a probabilistic prediction model whose mathematics must remain manageable.

BORE changes how expected improvement is computed by turning the problem into binary classification. The reformulation connects three quantities: class probabilities, ratios between probability densities, and expected improvement. Estimating class probabilities therefore provides a route to the density ratios needed to express the acquisition criterion. This makes classification machinery useful for guiding the optimization search.

The approach matters because requiring an analytically convenient predictive distribution can restrict the models available to Bayesian optimization. BORE bypasses those tractability constraints through its classification formulation. The paper identifies greater expressiveness, versatility, and scalability as advantages of this change, presenting a different computational route to expected improvement rather than a separate optimization objective.
icml-2021-bore-bayesian-optimization-by-.tldr: BORE reformulates expected improvement as binary classification, using density-ratio estimation to relax modeling constraints in Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: Offline model-based optimization seeks a high-scoring design using only a fixed collection of inputs and their measured outcomes. It is useful when gathering additional measurements is expensive or dangerous. The challenge is that searching for the best input to a learned scoring model can lead far from the examples on which that model was trained.

In those unfamiliar regions, erroneous overestimation can make a poor or invalid design look attractive. The optimizer then follows the model's mistakes. Conservative objective models address this problem by learning an objective model that lower-bounds the true score on inputs outside the training distribution and then optimizing using that conservative model.

The central idea is to make the learned scores useful for choosing designs under distributional shift, where optimistic errors can derail the search. The authors report that COMs outperform several existing methods across a range of problems, including controller parameters, robot morphologies, and superconducting materials. These findings support the approach across the evaluated offline optimization settings.
icml-2021-conservative-objective-models-.tldr: Conservative objective models counter overestimated scores on unfamiliar inputs to improve optimization from a fixed dataset.

paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model streams of discrete events whose occurrences are causally related over continuous time. Learning those relationships often assumes accurately recorded event times. This paper studies a more difficult observation setting: timestamps are displaced by random, unknown shifts introduced during event collection.

The authors prove that cumulants of these processes remain unchanged under random translations. Cumulants are statistical summaries, and their invariance provides information that survives this particular form of timing noise. Consequently, they can be used to learn the underlying causal structure even when the observed timestamps have been shifted. The result connects a mathematical property of the summaries directly to the structure-learning problem.

The paper also investigates how existing learning methods respond to random timestamp shifts. In the reported experiments, maximum likelihood estimators are brittle, whereas cumulant-based estimators remain stable even with substantial shifts. The theoretical and empirical findings therefore identify cumulants as a robust basis for learning under the specific timestamp corruption studied.
icml-2021-cumulants-of-hawkes-processes-.tldr: Cumulants preserve information about Hawkes-process causal structure under random timestamp shifts, and cumulant-based estimators show empirical stability.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks and biological vision models share useful principles, but conventional networks divide both space and depth into discrete units. That structure makes it difficult to capture continuously varying receptive field sizes and evolving neuronal responses. Deep continuous networks address this mismatch by making both spatial filtering and network depth continuous.

The architecture combines spatially continuous filters with the continuous-depth framework of neural ordinary differential equations. It can learn the spatial extent of its filters during training while modeling the continuous evolution of feature maps. These two features connect the network's representation and dynamics more closely to the biological models motivating the work.

The authors demonstrate image classification and reconstruction applications, reporting improved parameter and data efficiency and support for meta-parametrization. They also examine the biological plausibility of learned scale distributions and investigate a neuroscience-inspired pattern completion task. Finally, they explore an efficient implementation through changes in input contrast, extending the study from architectural principles to practical computation.
icml-2021-deep-continuous-networks-d905f.tldr: Deep continuous networks combine continuous spatial filters and neural ODE depth to learn filter scales and evolving visual representations.

paragraphs: Comparing many related high-dimensional datasets requires a distance that captures their internal geometry without making every comparison expensive. Diffusion Earth Mover's Distance represents each dataset as a distribution on a shared graph. That graph is constructed from affinities among the combined data, giving the distributions a common space for comparison.

When the graph discretizes a closed Riemannian manifold, the authors prove topological equivalence to standard Earth Mover's Distance using geodesic ground distance. This is a conditional relationship between the distances, not a claim that their numerical values coincide. Diffusion EMD has nearly linear computation time, is more accurate than similarly fast alternatives such as tree-based EMDs, and is fully differentiable.

The application uses single-cell data from 210 COVID-19 patient samples. Patient distances are computed at least two orders of magnitude faster than equally accurate methods. Embedding this distance matrix reveals patient structure and heterogeneity. Differentiability also makes the method suitable for possible future use in gradient-based learning frameworks.
icml-2021-diffusion-earth-movers-distanc.tldr: Diffusion EMD efficiently compares distributions on a shared data graph, with conditional geometric guarantees and a fast single-cell application.

paragraphs: Protein fragment libraries help structure prediction, simulation, and design by narrowing the enormous range of possible conformations. Existing generation methods can depend on related sequences or structures that are not readily available. The paper also identifies shortcomings in how those methods account for uncertainty from protein dynamics and experimental errors.

BIFROST approaches fragment generation as probabilistic modeling conditioned solely on the amino acid sequence. It combines a Deep Markov Model with directional statistics suited to angular variables and is implemented in Pyro. The generated quantities are backbone dihedral angles, allowing the model to describe possible fragment conformations probabilistically rather than relying on the additional biological information required by other approaches.

The authors report fragment libraries comparable in quality to those produced by state-of-the-art methods, generated in a fraction of the runtime. BIFROST also requires considerably less input information and supports efficient probability evaluation. Together, these properties make the contribution about both generating useful fragments and providing a computationally efficient probabilistic description of them.
icml-2021-efficient-generative-modelling.tldr: BIFROST generates competitive protein fragment libraries quickly using a probabilistic model conditioned only on amino acid sequences.

paragraphs: Euclidean projection finds the point in a permitted convex set that is closest to a given point. It appears in many constrained optimization procedures, but computing the projection can itself be expensive. This paper focuses on problems with smooth constraints and substantially fewer constraints than dimensions.

The authors propose a primal-dual method for this setting. Its runtime scales linearly with the dimension and logarithmically with the inverse of the requested accuracy. The abstract contrasts this with existing approaches whose runtime is either cubic in dimension or polynomial in inverse accuracy. Those dependencies matter because both high dimension and a demand for greater precision can otherwise make projection costly.

The contribution is therefore a more favorable computational scaling for a particular class of projection problems. The assumptions about smoothness and the relatively small number of constraints define the setting of the result. The paper also presents empirical performance comparisons with standard baselines, adding an experimental assessment to its runtime analysis.
icml-2021-fast-projection-onto-convex-sm.tldr: A primal-dual method accelerates projection with smooth convex constraints when the number of constraints is much smaller than the dimension.

paragraphs: Few-shot dataset generalization requires learning new classes from only a few examples in datasets not encountered during training. Training therefore draws on several diverse datasets to prepare a model for later adaptation. The challenge includes changes between datasets as well as the limited number of examples for each new classification task.

The paper proposes a universal template: a partially specified model that becomes specialized when suitable components are inserted. For a new task, adaptation only requires inferring a small number of parameters for those components. A separate network supplies an initial parameter setting based on the task, and a few gradient descent steps refine that initialization.

This design concentrates task-specific adaptation into a compact part of the model while using the diverse training collection to learn the shared template. The authors report greater parameter efficiency, scalability, and adaptability than previous methods, together with state-of-the-art results on Meta-Dataset. The findings support combining a reusable model structure with lightweight, task-dependent specialization.
icml-2021-learning-a-universal-template-.tldr: A universal model template adapts to new few-shot datasets by initializing and refining only a small set of task-specific parameters.

paragraphs: An agent following instructions may need to carry out behavior over time, respond to conditions, or choose among alternative ways to complete a task. LTL2Action expresses such instructions in linear temporal logic, a formal language that can describe these temporally extended requirements. The aim is to learn across many tasks and handle instructions absent from training.

The learning approach uses both the compositional structure of LTL expressions and their meaning. It trains task-conditioned policies, so the instruction helps determine the agent's behavior. The authors also introduce LTL pretraining that is independent of the downstream environment, reducing the overhead of learning the logic's semantics during environment-specific training.

Experiments cover discrete and continuous domains with combinatorial task sets containing up to approximately 10^39 unique tasks. They demonstrate learning to solve unseen tasks from LTL instructions, while the pretraining improves downstream sample efficiency. The large task-set size describes the combinatorial scope of the environments; the reported contribution is generalization through the structured instruction language.
icml-2021-ltl2action-generalizing-ltl-in.tldr: LTL2Action uses temporal logic structure and environment-independent pretraining to help reinforcement learning agents follow unseen instructions.

paragraphs: Variational auto-encoders learn latent-variable models by maximizing a lower bound on the evidence, known as the ELBO. A tighter bound can provide a better variational approximation. Importance sampling has been used toward this goal, but it is known to work poorly in high-dimensional settings, motivating more sophisticated sampling methods.

The paper examines two such methods: Annealed Importance Sampling and its Sequential Importance Sampling extensions. Their use in VAE training faces different obstacles. The AIS evidence estimate is difficult to differentiate, which complicates learning. SIS requires carefully selected backward Markov kernels, introducing another demanding part of the construction. These barriers had prevented the anticipated benefits from being realized for VAEs.

The authors address both obstacles and build the resulting Monte Carlo VAEs. They demonstrate the models across a variety of applications. The contribution is to make these more advanced evidence-estimation techniques usable within VAE learning, connecting improvements in sampling methodology to the practical requirements of optimizing the model.
icml-2021-monte-carlo-variational-auto-e.tldr: Monte Carlo VAEs address differentiation and backward-kernel obstacles that hinder advanced importance-sampling methods in VAE training.

paragraphs: Tensors organize data across multiple dimensions, and decomposition learns representations of the entities participating in those dimensions. Many real datasets are sparse, yet decomposition methods can explicitly or implicitly assume density. This paper makes sparsity part of the probabilistic model so that the pattern of observed entries can help shape the learned representations.

The construction begins with completely random measures defining tensor-valued random processes. The authors prove that the number of entries grows much more slowly than the corresponding tensor size, establishing sparsity. For finite observations, two decomposition models combine Dirichlet processes and Gaussian processes to generate entry locations and values jointly. Values depend nonlinearly on the embeddings, allowing structural and value information to inform them together.

For scalable learning, the paper combines stick-breaking constructions and random Fourier features in a stochastic variational algorithm. Experiments show advantages in generating sparse tensors and predicting entry indices and values in several real-world applications. The approach therefore treats sparse structure as information to model alongside nonlinear relationships between entities.
icml-2021-nonparametric-decomposition-of.tldr: A nonparametric tensor model jointly learns sparse entry patterns and nonlinear values to improve entity embeddings and prediction.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning has largely focused on identifying independent sources of variation. Real-world causal variables, however, can be statistically correlated. This paper studies what happens when prominent disentanglement methods encounter such correlations, examining whether the dependencies in the training data become dependencies in the learned latent representations.

The authors conduct an empirical study involving 4,260 models and systematically introduce correlations into datasets. They show and quantify that the models learn these correlations and reflect them in their latent representations. This matters for downstream applications such as fairness because the learned representation carries relationships present in the data rather than automatically separating them into independent factors.

The paper also demonstrates two ways to resolve latent correlations using supervision. One introduces weak supervision during training; the other corrects an already trained model using a small number of labels. The findings connect the behavior of disentanglement methods on correlated data with practical interventions available both during learning and after a model has been trained.
icml-2021-on-disentangled-representation.tldr: A large empirical study finds that disentanglement models absorb dataset correlations and demonstrates supervision-based ways to resolve them.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic learning in unknown Markov games when an agent cannot observe its opponents' actions. A natural benchmark is the best response one could have selected in hindsight. The authors show that achieving sublinear regret against this benchmark is statistically hard in the setting they consider.

They then adopt a weaker benchmark: the minimax value of the game. Against this value, their algorithm achieves regret of order K^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors, after K episodes. Because this grows more slowly than the number of episodes, average regret decreases with continued interaction. The result provides a learning guarantee despite the missing information about opponents' actions.

The bound does not depend on the sizes of the opponents' action spaces. This feature also matters when those actions are observable: the authors report an exponential improvement in the number of opponents over existing analysis. The guarantee remains tied to the minimax benchmark, preserving the distinction from the harder best-response-in-hindsight comparison.
icml-2021-online-learning-in-unknown-mar.tldr: An algorithm achieves sublinear regret against the minimax value in unknown Markov games without observing opponents' actions.

paragraphs: A few observed pixels usually leave many plausible images consistent with the available information. PixelTransformer models this uncertainty by inferring a distribution over an underlying spatial signal conditioned on sparse samples. The goal is to generate plausible possibilities and answer questions about unobserved locations from whatever samples are available.

The model permits conditioning on arbitrary samples and querying a distribution at any location. This flexibility distinguishes the approach from sequential autoregressive generation, where generation follows a sequence. Here, the observed locations can supply the conditioning information directly, making the relationship between sparse observations and the remaining signal central to the generative task.

Across three image datasets, the authors report diverse and meaningful generated samples. They also observe that distribution variance decreases as more pixels are supplied, reflecting reduced uncertainty with additional observations. Demonstrations extend beyond images to polynomials, three-dimensional shapes, and videos. These results support the approach as a model for several kinds of spatial signals rather than only image completion.
icml-2021-pixeltransformer-sample-condit.tldr: PixelTransformer generates spatial signals from arbitrary sparse observations and predicts distributions at requested locations.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs usually incorporate observations as samples from a joint data distribution. The paper calls this deterministic conditioning. In practice, available evidence may instead consist of marginal distributions, summary statistics, or a mechanism that generates samples. Conventional probabilistic programming systems do not adequately support modeling and inference for all these forms of information.

The authors introduce stochastic conditioning, which conditions on a variable's marginal distribution having a specified form. They formally define the concept, examine its properties, and show how to carry out inference with it. This expands the kinds of observational information that a probabilistic program can directly express and use in reasoning about its model.

Several case studies demonstrate potential uses involving different forms of stochastic conditioning and problems that are otherwise difficult to solve. The contribution includes both a formal description of the new conditioning operation and methods for working with it. Although developed within probabilistic programming, the authors state that the formalization is general enough to apply in other settings.
icml-2021-probabilistic-programs-with-st.tldr: Stochastic conditioning extends probabilistic programming to incorporate evidence about marginal distributions, with a formal definition and inference methods.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to use experience from previous tasks to make learning a new task faster or less data-intensive. A shared representation can provide that transferable knowledge. This paper develops theoretical foundations for such transfer in a specific setting: multiple linear regression tasks share a common low-dimensional linear representation.

The authors provide provably fast and sample-efficient algorithms for two linked problems. The first is discovering shared features from several related tasks. The second is using those features to learn previously unseen tasks. Studying both steps makes explicit how a representation is acquired and how it subsequently supports adaptation when data is scarce.

The paper also establishes information-theoretic lower bounds on the number of samples needed to learn the linear features. These complement the algorithmic guarantees by describing fundamental data requirements for the problem. The results supply a rigorous treatment of representation-based meta-learning within the shared linear model setting, where the structure connecting tasks is precisely specified.
icml-2021-provable-meta-learning-of-line.tldr: The paper gives efficient algorithms and sample-complexity lower bounds for learning and transferring shared linear representations across regression tasks.

paragraphs: Finding the best option in a stochastic bandit requires repeated measurements, but those measurements may share a divisible computing budget. Giving more resources to one measurement can finish it sooner while reducing total throughput because parallel speedups are imperfect. The paper studies how to allocate resources while learning which option is best.

For a fixed confidence target, the goal is to identify the best arm as quickly as possible. The proposed algorithm balances information accumulation against throughput. Its completion time is upper-bounded using a dynamic program whose inputs are the performance gaps between the optimal arm and the others. A matching hardness result complements this guarantee.

The paper also introduces an algorithm for a fixed deadline, where the objective is to maximize the probability of identifying the best arm before time runs out. Simulations show the algorithms consistently matching or outperforming the tested baselines across varied instances. The results connect statistical exploration decisions with the computational trade-offs governing how quickly evidence can be gathered.
icml-2021-resource-allocation-in-multi-a.tldr: Adaptive resource allocation balances measurement speed and throughput to improve best-arm identification under confidence or deadline requirements.

paragraphs: Gradient boosting can encounter loss functions with multiple modes, where reaching a local optimum does not establish that the best solution has been found. This paper introduces Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting to address that optimization difficulty. It presents the method as an efficient framework that may handle a broad range of losses.

SGLB is built from a form of the Langevin diffusion equation designed specifically for gradient boosting. This construction supports a theoretical guarantee of global convergence even for multimodal losses. The authors also provide generalization guarantees, addressing how the learned model performs beyond the optimization objective on its training data. These are distinct theoretical aspects of the proposed framework.

The empirical study considers classification with the 0-1 loss, which counts incorrect predictions and is multimodal in the setting described. SGLB outperforms classic gradient boosting in those experiments. The findings pair a theoretical treatment of global convergence with evidence on a classification loss that exhibits the optimization difficulty motivating the method.
icml-2021-sglb-stochastic-gradient-lange.tldr: SGLB adapts Langevin diffusion to gradient boosting, providing global convergence guarantees and improved reported performance on 0-1-loss classification.

paragraphs: Machine learning optimization often combines repeated passes through training examples with momentum, which incorporates information from earlier updates. This paper develops Shuffling Momentum Gradient for non-convex objectives expressed as finite sums. Although inspired by momentum, SMG uses an update that differs fundamentally from existing momentum methods.

The authors establish state-of-the-art convergence rates for any shuffling strategy with either constant or diminishing learning rates, assuming L-smoothness and bounded variance. The result therefore covers multiple ways of ordering the terms rather than depending on a single shuffling rule. The assumptions specify the regularity and variability conditions under which the rates hold.

For a fixed shuffling strategy, the paper introduces another algorithm closer to conventional momentum methods. It achieves the same convergence rates under L-smoothness and bounded gradients, a different set of assumptions. Numerical simulations on standard datasets compare both algorithms with existing shuffling methods and show encouraging performance, complementing the theoretical analysis without asserting universal empirical superiority.
icml-2021-smg-a-shuffling-gradient-based.tldr: SMG combines shuffling and a distinctive momentum update with convergence guarantees for non-convex finite-sum optimization under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian processes use inducing variables to make inference more manageable, and variational methods allow learning from mini-batches. However, increasing the number of inducing variables can still make computation expensive. This paper seeks to support large inducing sets without requiring the inducing inputs to have a specially structured arrangement.

The authors introduce a hierarchical prior that creates sparsity within the inducing-variable set itself. They use variational inference for the resulting model. In the experimental implementation, this sparsity is realized by considering the inducing inputs nearest to the data in a randomly selected mini-batch, connecting the computation to the local information relevant to that batch.

Experiments show considerable computational gains over standard sparse Gaussian processes, and broader validation demonstrates effectiveness against state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is an additional level of sparsity inside an already sparse approximation. This makes it possible to use a large overall collection of inducing points while avoiding the prohibitive computational cost that such a collection could otherwise impose.
icml-2021-sparse-within-sparse-gaussian-.tldr: A hierarchical prior and nearest-neighbor information add sparsity within inducing variables, enabling larger sparse Gaussian process models at lower computational cost.

paragraphs: High-performing vision transformers had relied on pretraining with hundreds of millions of images and substantial computing infrastructure. This paper demonstrates competitive convolution-free transformers trained using ImageNet alone, on one computer in less than three days. The work addresses the data and infrastructure demands that can make these architectures difficult to adopt.

The reference transformer contains 86 million parameters and reaches 83.1% single-crop top-1 accuracy on ImageNet without external data. The authors also introduce a teacher-student method tailored to transformers. A distillation token allows the student to learn from a teacher through attention, with a convolutional network typically serving as the teacher.

With the proposed approach, the learned transformers reach a reported 85.2% top-1 accuracy and are competitive with state-of-the-art ImageNet methods. They are similarly competitive when transferred to other tasks. The results demonstrate both a more accessible training setup and a way to communicate a teacher's knowledge through the transformer's attention mechanism, while keeping the student architecture convolution-free.
icml-2021-training-data-efficient-image-.tldr: ImageNet-only training and attention-based distillation produce competitive vision transformers without massive external pretraining datasets.

paragraphs: Some self-supervised methods learn useful representations by matching augmented views of the same example without using negative pairs from different examples. This raises a central question: why do the representations not collapse to a trivial output? The paper investigates the learning dynamics behind this behavior through a theoretical study of simple linear networks.

The analysis examines how predictor networks, stop-gradient operations, exponential moving averages, and weight decay interact. Although the networks studied are linear, their learning dynamics are nonlinear. The resulting theory reproduces findings from ablation studies on STL-10 and ImageNet and motivates a method that sets a linear predictor directly from its input statistics instead of training it through gradient updates.

On ImageNet, that predictor performs comparably to more complex two-layer nonlinear predictors using BatchNorm. The abstract reports improvements over a trained linear predictor of 2.5% after 300 epochs and 5% after 60 epochs. The contribution links a simplified account of collapse avoidance to a practical predictor construction supported by experiments.
icml-2021-understanding-self-supervised-.tldr: A linear-network analysis of non-contrastive learning motivates setting predictors from input statistics and helps explain representation collapse avoidance.
